classification.difficultyReason: Read the horizontal and vertical shifts directly from vertex form to identify the axis and vertex.

questions.mappingNote: Every part asks directly for axis and vertex from vertex form. The selected skill covers both requested features; intercepts are not requested.
questions.methodNote: The page 7 summary states that y=a(x-h)²+k, with a=1 or -1, has axis x=h and vertex (h,k). Examples b and c demonstrate this for reflected and translated parabolas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read the horizontal and vertical shifts directly from vertex form to identify the axis and vertex.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute x = 0 into each vertex-form equation and evaluate.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess algebraic calculation of a parabola's y-intercept. Parts a–c follow Example 1; parts d–f follow Example 2, with part f matching Example 2(c).
questions.methodNote: Example 1 on PDF page 5 and Example 2 on PDF page 7 find the y-intercept by setting x = 0, evaluating the squared bracket first, then applying the leading minus sign and vertical shift.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute x = 0 into each vertex-form equation and evaluate.

classification.difficultyReason: Use translations and substitution to sketch six upright parabolas with labelled vertices and y-intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts apply Example 1 directly to y=(x-h)²+k. The sketch is the assessed response, so sketch-parabola-from-equation is primary; translations support the method.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 on PDF page 5 identifies translations of y=x², obtains the vertex and axis of symmetry, substitutes x=0 for the y-intercept, and sketches the parabola using these features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use translations and substitution to sketch six upright parabolas with labelled vertices and y-intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch translated downward-opening parabolas using their vertices and calculated y-intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses sketching a translated downward-opening parabola, directly matching parabola-transformations; sketch-parabola-from-equation supports the required drawing.
questions.methodNote: Reflect the basic parabola in the x-axis, translate y=-x² to locate the vertex and symmetry axis, substitute x=0 for the y-intercept, and sketch using these features. Example 2 on pages 6–7 demonstrates this sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch translated downward-opening parabolas using their vertices and calculated y-intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply one horizontal or vertical translation to a given parabola, including symbolic distances.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess equations obtained by translating y=-x². The parabola-transformations skill covers both numerical and symbolic shifts.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes reflection to y=-x² and vertical shifts by adding or subtracting a constant. Page 4 establishes horizontal shifts by replacing x with x minus the rightward distance or x plus the leftward distance. Page 5 explicitly applies translation to y=-x².

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply one horizontal or vertical translation to a given parabola, including symbolic distances.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught horizontal and vertical translation rules directly to y=x², using numerical or symbolic distances without an additional inference.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts apply the combined translation method directly to y=x²; the final two parts generalise the same rules to symbolic distances.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 derives vertical translations by adding or subtracting the vertical distance. Page 4 derives horizontal translations using x minus the rightward distance or x plus the leftward distance, then combines horizontal and vertical translations. Example 1 on page 5 applies these rules to vertex-form equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the taught horizontal and vertical translation rules directly to y=x², using numerical or symbolic distances without an additional inference.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch a translated parabola and compose numerical and symbolic translations.

questions.mappingNote: The initial sketch uses the taught vertex and intercept method. Parts a–c compose further translations of the given parabola, including symbolic horizontal and vertical displacements.
questions.methodNote: Vertical and horizontal translations move the vertex while preserving the basic parabola's shape. Page 4 combines translations; Example 1 on page 5 sketches using the vertex, symmetry axis and substitution x=0.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch a translated parabola and compose numerical and symbolic translations.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that a y-intercept has x=0, evaluate the fixed square to obtain y=1+a, then subtract 1 from each supplied intercept. All four parts repeat this direct procedure.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess the relationship between a parabola's equation and its y-intercept, with an unknown vertical translation.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 on PDF page 5 finds a y-intercept by substituting x = 0 into vertex form. Apply that substitution and solve the resulting equation for a.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that a y-intercept has x=0, evaluate the fixed square to obtain y=1+a, then subtract 1 from each supplied intercept. All four parts repeat this direct procedure.

classification.difficultyReason: Set x=0 at the y-intercept, evaluate the square while retaining the leading minus sign to obtain y=-4+b, then add 4 to each supplied intercept. The parts repeat the same direct procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Each part applies the same substitution to y = −(x − 2)² + b, then solves for b from the given intercept. Finding a parabola's intercept is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 2(c) on PDF page 7 finds the y-intercept of y = −(x − 2)² + 6 by substituting x = 0, evaluating the square and retaining the leading minus sign.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Set x=0 at the y-intercept, evaluate the square while retaining the leading minus sign to obtain y=-4+b, then add 4 to each supplied intercept. The parts repeat the same direct procedure.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch rotations of the basic parabola, including an oblique axis of symmetry.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts extend the explicitly illustrated rotation method to different angles or directions. Parabola transformations is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: The teaching rotates the basic parabola about the origin, retaining its vertex and rotating its axis of symmetry; it illustrates 45-degree and 90-degree clockwise rotations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch rotations of the basic parabola, including an oblique axis of symmetry.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines substitution, reading vertex form, sketching and interpreting intercept counts.

questions.mappingNote: Each supplied equation is already in vertex form; sketching and feature identification are directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: Substitute x=0, read the vertex and axis from completed-square form, sketch with the correct concavity and infer the number of crossings.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines substitution, reading vertex form, sketching and interpreting intercept counts.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied sequence to complete the square, identify the intercept, axis and vertex, sketch with the correct concavity, and infer the number of crossings from the extremum. These are routine linked procedures; fractional vertices and negative leading coefficients require sign care but no unsignposted reframing.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess the taught completed-square sketching procedure. Parts g–i and l require exact fractions.
questions.methodNote: Add and subtract the square of half the linear coefficient; for a negative leading coefficient, factor out −1 first. Read vertex and axis, substitute x=0 and sketch; infer root counts without finding roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied sequence to complete the square, identify the intercept, axis and vertex, sketch with the correct concavity, and infer the number of crossings from the extremum. These are routine linked procedures; fractional vertices and negative leading coefficients require sign care but no unsignposted reframing.

classification.difficultyReason: Finds roots from vertex form, including exact simplified surds and negative leading signs.

questions.mappingNote: Every equation is already completed-square form; intercept solving is the most advanced directly assessed feature.
questions.methodNote: Set y=0, isolate the squared expression, take both square roots, then solve for x and simplify surds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Finds roots from vertex form, including exact simplified surds and negative leading signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the specified completing-the-square method, set y=0 and take both square roots; negative leading coefficients require factoring out −1 and some roots require surd simplification.

questions.mappingNote: Completing the square to solve is explicitly required; factoring or the quadratic formula would bypass the assessed method.
questions.methodNote: Follow Example 5: complete the square, factoring −1 first where necessary, substitute y=0 and take both square roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the specified completing-the-square method, set y=0 and take both square roots; negative leading coefficients require factoring out −1 and some roots require surd simplification.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied five-step sequence scaffolds routine completion of the square, extraction of features, exact root solving and sketching; students must interpret whether the completed square permits real intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses the full algebraic feature-based sketching process. Odd coefficients require exact fractional vertices and several roots remain surds.
questions.methodNote: Follow Example 5 in order: substitute x=0; complete the square, factoring −1 first when needed; read vertex and axis; set y=0 and use both square roots, or explain why there are no real roots; sketch and mark features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The supplied five-step sequence scaffolds routine completion of the square, extraction of features, exact root solving and sketching; students must interpret whether the completed square permits real intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch each supplied y=kx² curve on shared axes using its common vertex, symmetry, coefficient sign and relative width, with simple substituted points. The positive coefficient in b(iii) requires an upward-opening curve. These are direct applications of taught transformations without an unsignposted connection.

questions.mappingNote: Each set directly compares y=kx² on shared axes. Parabola transformations is the closest catalogue skill; completing the square and finding an equation from features are not required.
questions.methodNote: Pages 14–15 compare y=3x² with y=x² by multiplying ordinates and discuss reflection in the x-axis for negative coefficients. Pages 16–18 reinforce identifying the vertex, axis and opening direction before sketching. The vertex-and-point example on page 19 is context rather than the method assessed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch each supplied y=kx² curve on shared axes using its common vertex, symmetry, coefficient sign and relative width, with simple substituted points. The positive coefficient in b(iii) requires an upward-opening curve. These are direct applications of taught transformations without an unsignposted connection.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine exact intercept calculations with labelled sketches of upward- and downward-opening parabolas.

questions.mappingNote: Each assigned equation already has the form y=kx²+c. The directly assessed skill is sketching these parabolas from vertex, intercepts and concavity; completing the square is unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: The introduction and translations of y=3x² establish vertical scaling, vertical translation, symmetry and vertex position. Example 6 finds y-intercepts by substituting x=0, identifies the vertex and concavity, and finds x-intercepts by setting y=0 and taking both square roots. The summary and Example 7 reinforce sketching from these features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine exact intercept calculations with labelled sketches of upward- and downward-opening parabolas.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that translations preserve the quadratic coefficient and reflection reverses its sign, then classify twelve parabolas.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 directly applies the translation and reflection discussion: compare the absolute quadratic coefficients rather than calculate intercepts or vertices.
questions.methodNote: Pages 14–15 introduce vertical stretching and translations of y=3x², extending the discussion to negative coefficients through reflection in the x-axis. Page 18 states that y=ax²+bx+c is a translation of, and congruent to, y=ax².

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that translations preserve the quadratic coefficient and reflection reverses its sign, then classify twelve parabolas.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square after factoring out a non-unit coefficient, including fractional shifts and a negative leading coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess rewriting a non-monic quadratic in completed-square form; no sketch or feature calculation is requested.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 factors out the leading coefficient, adds and subtracts the square of half the remaining x coefficient inside brackets, then expands the constant term.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square after factoring out a non-unit coefficient, including fractional shifts and a negative leading coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete non-monic squares, determine exact intercepts and combine the features in sketches.

questions.mappingNote: Every part requires a complete sketch from algebraically derived features, so sketch-parabola-from-equation is the primary skill. Completing the square and identifying intercepts, axis and vertex are directly assessed supporting skills.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 on pages 16–17 factors out the leading coefficient, adds and subtracts the square of half the remaining linear coefficient, and reads the vertex and symmetry axis from completed-square form. Substitute x=0 for the y-intercept and y=0 for any x-intercepts. Use the minimum or maximum to explain absent intercepts, then sketch.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete non-monic squares, determine exact intercepts and combine the features in sketches.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute signed coefficients into the axis formula, calculate fractional vertex coordinates and use concavity to decide whether x-intercepts exist.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess the axis formula, vertex substitution and the existence of intercepts. The closest catalogue skill is parabola-intercepts-axis-vertex. No intercept coordinates or sketches are requested.
questions.methodNote: Pages 17–18 derive x=-b/(2a). Page 18, Example 7, substitutes the axis value into the original quadratic to obtain the vertex, then uses concavity and the vertex height to determine whether x-intercepts exist.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute signed coefficients into the axis formula, calculate fractional vertex coordinates and use concavity to decide whether x-intercepts exist.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the supplied y-intercept at x = 0 and solve a linear equation for the unknown constant.

questions.mappingNote: Each part supplies the point (0, y-intercept), so substitution in the given vertex form determines k. Finding an equation from supplied features is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 evaluates the y-intercept by setting x = 0. Example 8 substitutes a known point into vertex form and solves for the unknown parameter.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the supplied y-intercept at x = 0 and solve a linear equation for the unknown constant.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute each supplied y-intercept into vertex form and solve a linear equation for the coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: This question determines the unknown coefficient from a supplied intercept in vertex form; find-equation-parabola-features is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 on PDF page 19 substitutes a known point into vertex form and solves for a. At a y-intercept the known point has x=0, as illustrated by the intercept calculations on pages 17–18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute each supplied y-intercept into vertex form and solve a linear equation for the coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the y-intercept into vertex form and solve for both possible values of the horizontal parameter.

questions.mappingNote: Each part determines the horizontal parameter in a supplied parabola equation from its y-intercept. Finding a parabola equation from features is the closest catalogue skill; solving ax²=c is also directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: Substitute x=0 for a y-intercept, as demonstrated in Example 6; determine the unknown parameter by substitution into vertex form, following Example 8. Solve the resulting square equation with both signs, consistent with Example 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the y-intercept into vertex form and solve for both possible values of the horizontal parameter.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the given vertex to construct vertex form and substitute the other point to determine its coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 supplies a vertex and one other point, directly matching Example 8. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same complete source task.
questions.methodNote: Page 19, Example 8: write y=a(x-h)^2+k using the vertex, substitute the other point and solve for a.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the given vertex to construct vertex form and substitute the other point to determine its coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the given vertex to construct vertex form, then substitute another point to determine the coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Question 11 directly assesses this method with vertex (-2,-1) and point (1,26); the closest catalogue skill is finding a parabola's equation from features.
questions.methodNote: Page 19, Example 8, constructs y=a(x-h)^2+k from the vertex and substitutes the other point to determine a.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the given vertex to construct vertex form, then substitute another point to determine the coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the vertex to establish vertex form and substitute the y-intercept to determine the coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied vertex determines h=1 and k=6; the y-intercept supplies the other point (0,4). Determining the equation from these features directly assesses find-equation-parabola-features.
questions.methodNote: Page 19 introduces finding an equation from the vertex and another point: write y=a(x-h)^2+k and substitute the other point to find a, as demonstrated in Example 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the vertex to establish vertex form and substitute the y-intercept to determine the coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Read vertex form, solve for exact intercepts and combine the features in a sketch.

questions.mappingNote: Every part is already in vertex form, including g after reordering its terms. The task directly assesses sketching from algebraically determined features; the intercept/axis/vertex skill is secondary. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and cannot be reused.
questions.methodNote: Read (h,k) and x=h from y=a(x-h)^2+k, use the sign of a for concavity, substitute x=0 for the y-intercept and solve y=0 using square roots. Sketch using these features, as in Example 6 and the vertex-form summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read vertex form, solve for exact intercepts and combine the features in a sketch.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the vertex's x-coordinate by averaging two given x-intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses the vertex's x-coordinate from given intercepts, so parabola-intercepts-axis-vertex is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 finds the axis of symmetry by averaging the two x-intercepts; the vertex has that same x-coordinate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the vertex's x-coordinate by averaging two given x-intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the vertex's x-coordinate by averaging two given x-intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses one parabola feature from two supplied intercepts; no equation, y-coordinate or sketch is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the average of the two x-intercepts to locate the axis of symmetry and hence the vertex's x-coordinate, as demonstrated in Example 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the vertex's x-coordinate by averaging two given x-intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Read roots from factors, average them to locate the axis, substitute for the vertex and sketch each parabola.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts require algebraic features and a sketch from a factorised equation, so sketch-parabola-from-equation is the primary skill. Example 10 concerns constructing an equation and is not needed here.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 sets x=0 for the y-intercept and y=0 for the roots, averages the two roots for the axis, then substitutes that x-coordinate for the vertex. Concavity follows from the sign of the quadratic coefficient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read roots from factors, average them to locate the axis, substitute for the vertex and sketch each parabola.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor monic and non-monic quadratics, differences of squares and common-factor expressions, then apply the null factor law to find intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 explicitly refers to Example 9. Parts a–d use monic binomial factors; e uses non-monic factorisation; f–g use differences of squares; h–i use a common factor. All nine then use the null factor law. Sketching, vertex calculations and y-intercepts are not requested.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 finds x-intercepts by setting y=0 and using factored form. Its parts b and c demonstrate factorisation before identifying roots; part e demonstrates exact fractional and surd intercepts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factor monic and non-monic quadratics, differences of squares and common-factor expressions, then apply the null factor law to find intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Factorise monic and non-monic quadratics, average their roots to locate the axis, calculate the vertex and sketch all requested features.

questions.mappingNote: Every assigned part requests a sketch labelled with intercepts, symmetry axis and vertex; sketch-parabola-from-equation is the most advanced directly assessed skill. Example 10 on page 23 concerns finding an equation and is not needed for this task.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 finds the y-intercept by substituting x=0, factorises to find the x-intercepts, averages the x-intercepts for the symmetry axis and substitutes this x-value for the vertex. Concavity follows from the sign of the quadratic coefficient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factorise monic and non-monic quadratics, average their roots to locate the axis, calculate the vertex and sketch all requested features.

classification.difficultyReason: Read two roots and another point from each graph, then determine the coefficient by substitution.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires reading the two roots and a third point, applying Example 10, and expanding the resulting factorised equation.
questions.methodNote: Page 23 explicitly gives y=a(x-u)(x-v), then substitutes another known point to find a. Example 10 demonstrates this with a y-intercept; pages 21–22 establish intercept and symmetry features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read two roots and another point from each graph, then determine the coefficient by substitution.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine a factorised equation from two roots and a point away from the axes.

questions.mappingNote: The additional point is (4,10), so substitution uses x=4 rather than the y-intercept substitution in the example.
questions.methodNote: Use the roots as factors and substitute another point to determine a, as stated and demonstrated in Example 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine a factorised equation from two roots and a point away from the axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Use two roots and a y-intercept to determine a fractional leading coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly follows Example 10, with roots -2 and 3 and vertical intercept -3.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 forms factors from the roots and substitutes x=0 with the given y-intercept to determine a.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use two roots and a y-intercept to determine a fractional leading coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Form factors including a fractional root, then substitute a point to determine the coefficient exactly.

questions.mappingNote: The fractional root is retained exactly as x-1/2; substituting (1,-3) determines a=6.
questions.methodNote: Form y=a(x-u)(x-v), then determine a by substituting the supplied point, following the rule preceding Example 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form factors including a fractional root, then substitute a point to determine the coefficient exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose efficient algebraic methods from the discriminant, calculate exact features and construct labelled sketches across twelve quadratics.

questions.mappingNote: The complete twelve-part task directly assesses selecting and combining these methods to sketch a parabola. Sketching is the primary skill; discriminant classification and algebraic features are supporting skills.
questions.methodNote: Pages 24–26 teach discriminant classification, factorisation for rational intercepts, the quadratic formula for irrational intercepts, x=-b/(2a) or the midpoint of roots for the axis, substitution for the vertex ordinate, and labelled sketches. Pages 27–28 begin unrelated applications and are reference context only.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose efficient algebraic methods from the discriminant, calculate exact features and construct labelled sketches across twelve quadratics.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent related rectangle dimensions algebraically, form an area equation and reject a negative solution.

questions.mappingNote: The paddock task requires forming and solving a quadratic area equation from related dimensions, rather than optimising an area. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines an unknown dimension, expresses related lengths, forms and factorises a quadratic, then rejects an inadmissible length. Page 28 models rectangle dimensions and area algebraically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent related rectangle dimensions algebraically, form an area equation and reject a negative solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the equal base and perpendicular height by one variable, apply the triangle area formula, take a square root and select the positive length.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 applies the same modelling sequence to equal base and perpendicular height in the triangle area formula; solving the resulting quadratic gives the positive base length.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines an unknown length, forms a quadratic from a geometric formula and rejects a geometrically inadmissible solution. Page 28 reinforces forming area expressions from dimensions and interpreting solutions in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent the equal base and perpendicular height by one variable, apply the triangle area formula, take a square root and select the positive length.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent consecutive positive integers algebraically, factorise the resulting quadratic and reject the negative solution.

questions.mappingNote: Representing consecutive integers by n and n+1 produces a monic quadratic. Modelling and interpreting the positive solution directly assesses quadratic word problems.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines an unknown, forms a quadratic from the context, rearranges and factorises it, then rejects a root that violates the problem's requirements. Page 28 reiterates that algebraic solutions must satisfy the practical conditions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent consecutive positive integers algebraically, factorise the resulting quadratic and reject the negative solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Model consecutive even numbers, factorise the resulting quadratic and interpret both solutions.

questions.mappingNote: Representing consecutive even numbers by x and x+2 directly assesses modelling and solving a quadratic word problem. Neither negative root nor negative numbers are excluded by this task.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines an unknown, forms a quadratic, factorises and checks each solution against the context. Page 28 reiterates that admissibility depends on the question's requirements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model consecutive even numbers, factorise the resulting quadratic and interpret both solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Model consecutive odd integers with a quadratic and interpret both valid solution pairs.

questions.mappingNote: Representing consecutive odd numbers as x and x+2 directly assesses quadratic modelling. Unlike triangle side lengths, negative odd numbers are admissible in this printed task.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines an unknown, forms a quadratic from the context, factorises and checks which roots satisfy the original conditions. Page 28 reinforces that admissibility depends on the question's requirements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model consecutive odd integers with a quadratic and interpret both valid solution pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a verbal relationship into a quadratic equation, factorise and reject the negative solution.

questions.mappingNote: The verbal number relationship requires forming and solving a quadratic, then using the positive-number condition to select the admissible solution.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines an unknown, forms a quadratic equation, factorises and rejects a solution that fails the context. Page 28 reiterates that algebraic solutions must satisfy the requirements of the question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a verbal relationship into a quadratic equation, factorise and reject the negative solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate an age relationship into a quadratic, factorise and reject the negative age.

questions.mappingNote: The age statement requires modelling with x² = x + 56 and interpreting the factorised solutions in context, directly assessing quadratic word problems.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines an unknown, forms a quadratic from the context, factorises, applies the null factor law and rejects an inadmissible solution. Page 28 reiterates that algebraic solutions must satisfy the practical requirements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate an age relationship into a quadratic, factorise and reject the negative age.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the savings relationship into a non-monic quadratic, factorise and reject the negative solution in context.

questions.mappingNote: The squared-and-doubled savings relationship requires forming and solving a quadratic and interpreting its roots. No geometric diagram is needed for this numerical relationship.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines an unknown, forms a quadratic from the context, rearranges and factorises, then rejects a solution that does not satisfy the physical requirements. Page 28 reiterates that algebraic solutions may be inadmissible.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate the savings relationship into a non-monic quadratic, factorise and reject the negative solution in context.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent related perpendicular sides algebraically, form a quadratic using Pythagoras’ theorem and reject an inadmissible root.

questions.mappingNote: This task uses the same triangle-modelling and root-rejection method, with perpendicular sides x and x+7 and a known hypotenuse of 17 cm. Modelling and solving the resulting quadratic is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 on page 27 defines unknown triangle side lengths, applies Pythagoras’ theorem, expands and factorises the resulting quadratic, then rejects a root giving an impossible side length. Page 28 reiterates that contextual restrictions can exclude algebraic solutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent related perpendicular sides algebraically, form a quadratic using Pythagoras’ theorem and reject an inadmissible root.
